summary: Proposes the syntax of the Network Access Identifier, the user identity string submitted during PPP authentication, normally written like a username at a realm. It helps roaming users be routed to the right place. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 4282.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like a name tag with your name and your home organization. A network reads it to know where to check who you are.

questions: what is a network access identifier
how does nai help with internet roaming
what is the difference between username and realm
subtitle: A standardized format for user identity during internet roaming and tunneling.

tldr.problem: When internet users roam across multiple service providers or use corporate VPNs, systems need a standard way to identify the user and route authentication requests to the right home provider.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Access Identifier uses the format user@realm, similar to an email address, where the realm identifies the user's home authentication server.
tldr.outcome: Roaming users can use any dial-up access point from a consortium of ISPs and be correctly routed for authentication. It was superseded by RFC 4282.

today: RFC 2486 defined the NAI for the roaming era of the late 1990s and early 2000s. It was updated and superseded by RFC 4282, which refined the specification and addressed implementation experience. NAI format is still used in modern authentication protocols like EAP.

sections.title: Roaming and the Identity Problem
sections.content:
In the 1990s, internet access was typically tied to a single Internet Service Provider (ISP). A customer would dial into their ISP and be authenticated by that ISP's servers. But as internet use grew, users wanted to dial into any convenient ISP—whether a regional provider, a national provider, or a partner in another country—while maintaining their relationship with their home ISP.

The problem: when a user dials into an unfamiliar access point and provides a username and password, how does the access point know where to send the authentication request? The username alone could be ambiguous (many 'john' accounts exist). The system needs to identify not just the username but the realm—the home domain or organization where that user's account lives.

This need applies both to dial-up internet roaming (where a user can access the internet through any cooperating ISP) and to tunneling services like VPNs (where a user can tunnel securely into a corporate intranet through any ISP's connection).
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine you can log into the internet through any ISP in your region, not just your own. Your home ISP needs to recognize you wherever you dial in. So you have to tell the access point not just your name, but which home ISP you belong to.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
The Network Access Identifier (NAI) is the user ID submitted by the client during PPP authentication. It serves two purposes: to identify the user and to help route the authentication request to the correct authentication server.

The Network Access Server (NAS) is the equipment at the dial-in point that accepts connections from users. In PPTP terminology it is called the PAC (PPTP Access Concentrator); in L2TP it is called the LAC (L2TP Access Concentrator).

Roaming capability is the ability to use any one of several ISPs while maintaining a customer relationship with only one. Examples include regional ISP consortia, national ISPs cooperating internationally, and enterprises providing global dial-in access to employees.

A tunneling service uses protocols like PPTP, L2F, L2TP, or IPsec to create secure connections. The NAI helps route the initial authentication that establishes the tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things to know: the NAI is your identifier, the NAS is the access point you dial into, and roaming is being able to use different ISPs while staying a customer of one home ISP.

sections.title: The NAI Format
sections.content:
The NAI has the form username@realm. Examples include fred@3com.com, nancy@eng.bigu.edu, and eng%nancy@bigu.edu. The username portion uses a dot-string syntax that allows letters, digits, and special characters except space and certain reserved symbols.

The realm portion is a fully qualified domain name (FQDN). Unlike DNS, which does not allow realm names to start with a digit, the NAI standard explicitly allows FQDNs like 3com.com to start with a number, reflecting real-world practice.

The ABNF grammar is formal and precise: a username is a dot-string (dots separate sub-components), each component is a string of ASCII characters, and characters can be escaped with backslash. The realm is a series of labels separated by dots, each label containing alphanumerics and hyphens.

Implementors must ensure their systems support NAIs of at least 72 octets in length. The NAI is meant for machine processing in authentication protocols like RADIUS, not necessarily for human entry, though it resembles an email address.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is simple: a username, an @ sign, and a domain name. The domain name is like an email domain. Some special characters are allowed in the username, but spaces are not.

sections.title: Realm Administration and the DNS Link
sections.content:
The NAI realm namespace must be unique, just like the DNS namespace. To avoid conflicts, the RFC proposes piggybacking NAI administration on top of DNS administration. An organization wishing to use an NAI realm for roaming must first acquire rights to a corresponding fully qualified domain name.

This design prevents collisions: if alice@example.com is an NAI in some roaming consortium, only the organization that owns example.com can issue that NAI. The NAI realm name does not imply that the DNS is used to locate the authentication server—existing roaming implementations used local proxy configuration files—but the uniqueness guarantee is valuable.

Using an FQDN as a realm name does not mean the NAI must be a valid email address, or that the username portion follows email conventions. Some NAIs may look like email addresses, but they are not required to be.
sections.plainLanguage: The realm part of an NAI looks like a web domain, and that is intentional: it uses the same uniqueness rules as DNS to make sure no two organizations use the same realm.

viz.caption: Examples of Valid and Invalid NAIs

data.title: NAI Format Examples
data.code:
Valid:
  fred@3com.com
  fred@foo-9.com
  fred_smith@big-co.com
  fred=?#$&*+-/^smith@bigco.com
  eng!nancy@bigu.edu
  eng%nancy@bigu.edu

Invalid:
  fred@foo (missing dot in realm)
  fred@foo_9.com (underscore in domain label)
  @howard.edu (missing username)
  fred@bigco.com@smallco.com (multiple @)
  eng:nancy@bigu.edu (colon not allowed)
